questions.q: A sale happens on June 1st, but because of a POS sync delay, it doesn't reach the source system until June 2nd's export file. Which source file does incremental Bronze ingestion read it from?
options: June 1st's file — ingestion goes back and rewrites the original file
It gets discarded because its sale_date doesn't match the file's date
It gets duplicated into both June 1st's and June 2nd's Bronze partitions
June 2nd's file — because that's the new file ingestion actually picks up that day
questions.explain: Incremental ingestion reads whatever new file physically landed; the late sale is inside June 2nd's file, so that's where Bronze picks it up, with its original sale_date column intact.

questions.q: Once the late sale is in Bronze, what determines where it lands in silver.sales_clean?
options: Alphabetical order of store_id
Its transaction_id, matched against existing rows in the MERGE INTO statement — not the date it was ingested
The file name it arrived in
Whatever today's system date happens to be
questions.explain: The MERGE INTO matches ON transaction_id. Since this transaction_id has never been seen before, it hits WHEN NOT MATCHED and is inserted with its real sale_date untouched.

questions.q: Why does this late sale correctly end up in June 1st's Gold totals, even though it arrived in the pipeline on June 2nd?
options: Because Gold tables aggregate GROUP BY sale_date, which reflects when the sale actually happened, not when it was loaded
Because Bronze automatically moves late rows into the correct day's partition
Because Gold tables have a special late-arrival correction step
Because the watermark table meta.last_ingested_date overwrites sale_date
questions.explain: Both Gold tables group by sale_date (the business date), so whenever Gold recomputes from Silver's current state, the late row folds into the day it actually happened, with no special-case logic needed.

questions.q: What would go wrong under a naive design that matched the Silver MERGE on sale_date instead of transaction_id?
options: Bronze ingestion would fail to read the file at all
The late June 1st sale could collapse into or overwrite an unrelated row already dated June 1st, since many transactions share the same sale_date
The MERGE statement would throw a syntax error
Nothing — sale_date and transaction_id are interchangeable as match keys
questions.explain: sale_date is shared by many transactions, so using it as a match key risks silently merging distinct sales together — exactly the mistake Lesson 5 warns against.

questions.q: What would go wrong under a naive design that stamped incoming rows with "today's date" instead of preserving their real sale_date?
options: The transaction_id of the late sale would change
The sale would be dropped from Bronze entirely
Gold totals would be correct for both days, since total dollar amounts never change
The late sale would be counted in June 2nd's Gold totals instead of June 1st's, inflating June 2nd and under-counting June 1st
questions.explain: Overwriting sale_date with the load date would misattribute the sale to the wrong day's aggregation, silently inflating one day's total and under-counting the other.
